layers.name: Bash / User Process
layers.description: User command line, parsing, fork/exec, stdio redirection.

layers.name: Syscall & VFS
layers.description: Syscall trap, path walk, inode lookup, VFS abstractions.

layers.name: ext4 Filesystem
layers.description: Inodes, extents, block bitmaps, directory entries.

layers.name: Page Cache & Writeback
layers.description: Dirty/clean page lifecycle in the cache.

layers.name: NVMe Driver / NCQ
layers.description: Queueing requests and talking over PCIe.

layers.name: NAND Flash
layers.description: Physical cells programmed/erased in pages and blocks.

steps.title: User types command and presses Enter
steps.description: In a terminal, the user types a command like echo "Hello world" > newfile and hits Enter.
steps.kernelDetails: No kernel involvement yet beyond terminal I/O.
steps.hardwareDetails: Characters buffered by terminal emulator and pty.

steps.title: Bash reads the command line
steps.description: Bash reads the input line (typically via readline), handling history, quoting, and editing.
steps.kernelDetails: read() on stdin delivers characters to bash.
steps.hardwareDetails: Data flows from keyboard to terminal to bash process.

steps.title: Bash parses, expands, and sets up redirection
steps.description: Bash tokenizes the line, performs expansions (variables, globs), and notes that '>' redirects stdout to a file with O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC flags.
steps.kernelDetails: Still in user space; preparing for later open().
steps.hardwareDetails: No disk I/O yet.

steps.title: Bash forks a child for the command
steps.description: For an external binary or redirection, bash calls fork() to create a child that inherits its environment and file descriptor table.
steps.kernelDetails: fork() duplicates the process, copying metadata and mappings.
steps.hardwareDetails: RAM allocations and page table updates; no SSD access.

steps.title: Child execve() loads the binary and sets up fds
steps.description: In the child, bash uses execve() to load the program (e.g., /bin/echo) and sets up file descriptors so stdout points to the file to be created.
steps.kernelDetails: execve() loads the ELF binary and prepares the new process image.
steps.hardwareDetails: Instruction and data fetches from storage via the page cache (not shown in this flow).

steps.title: Program runs and will issue syscalls
steps.description: The user program starts executing its main() and will soon call open(), write(), and close() via libc wrappers.
steps.kernelDetails: User space prepares to cross the kernel boundary.
steps.hardwareDetails: CPU executes user instructions in ring 3.

steps.title: Resolve pathname in user space
steps.description: The program resolves the pathname, possibly calling getcwd() and building a relative or absolute path for newfile.
steps.kernelDetails: libc helpers may use getcwd() or cached working directory state.
steps.hardwareDetails: No direct disk access yet; purely user-space string work.

steps.title: Issue open() syscall with O_CREAT
steps.description: The program calls open("newfile", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC, 0644) or creat() for touch-like behavior.
steps.kernelDetails: libc wrapper enters kernel via openat() or open().
steps.hardwareDetails: CPU prepares to transition to kernel mode.

steps.title: Trap into kernel mode
steps.description: The CPU executes the syscall instruction, switching from user mode to kernel mode and jumping to the syscall entry point.
steps.kernelDetails: Syscall entry saves registers and sets up a kernel stack frame.
steps.hardwareDetails: Control stays on CPU; no storage access yet.

steps.title: Syscall dispatcher routes to do_sys_open()
steps.description: The kernel's syscall dispatcher examines the syscall number and dispatches to do_sys_open() → do_filp_open() → path_openat().
steps.kernelDetails: VFS open helpers begin processing the request.
steps.hardwareDetails: Still CPU-bound; no disk I/O yet.

steps.title: VFS pathname resolution via namei
steps.description: VFS walks the path with link_path_walk(), consulting dentry and inode caches. The parent directory is found; the final component is a negative dentry.
steps.kernelDetails: Dentry and inode caches accelerate path resolution.
steps.hardwareDetails: If cached, no immediate disk I/O is needed.

steps.title: Permission and policy checks
steps.description: The kernel checks directory permissions and security policies using inode_permission(), POSIX ACLs, and SELinux or other LSM hooks.
steps.kernelDetails: Access checks ensure the caller can create in this directory.
steps.hardwareDetails: No SSD interactions; purely in-memory metadata checks.

steps.title: Invoke ext4_create() for filesystem-specific work
steps.description: The VFS calls inode->i_op->create(), which for ext4 is ext4_create(), transferring control into the ext4 driver.
steps.kernelDetails: Filesystem-specific create logic is now active.
steps.hardwareDetails: Subsequent steps may read or update on-disk metadata.

steps.title: Allocate a new ext4 inode
steps.description: ext4_new_inode() scans the inode bitmap for a free inode, marks it allocated, and initializes mode, UID, GID, and timestamps.
steps.kernelDetails: On-disk inode structures are prepared for the new file.
steps.hardwareDetails: May require reading and later writing inode bitmap blocks.

steps.title: Create a directory entry for the new file
steps.description: ext4_add_entry() updates the parent directory block (or htree) to map the new filename to its inode number.
steps.kernelDetails: Directory data structures are modified in memory.
steps.hardwareDetails: Associated directory blocks will later be written to SSD.

steps.title: Start a JBD2 journal transaction for metadata
steps.description: jbd2_journal_start() begins a transaction covering inode, directory entry, and bitmap updates. In data=ordered mode, only metadata is journaled.
steps.kernelDetails: Journal buffers capture pending metadata changes.
steps.hardwareDetails: Journal blocks reside on the same SSD, written sequentially.

steps.title: Commit the journal transaction for create
steps.description: jbd2_journal_commit_transaction() writes the journal commit record, ensuring that after a crash, the create is either fully applied or fully rolled back.
steps.kernelDetails: Commit block marks the end of this transaction.
steps.hardwareDetails: SSD receives sequential journal writes before metadata replay.

steps.title: Instantiate VFS dentry and file structures
steps.description: dentry_open() sets up in-memory dentry and inode objects and creates a struct file representing the open file.
steps.kernelDetails: These structures live only in kernel memory.
steps.hardwareDetails: No further disk I/O; purely in-memory bookkeeping.

steps.title: Allocate a file descriptor slot
steps.description: get_unused_fd_flags() finds a free file descriptor number in the process's fd table and associates it with the new struct file.
steps.kernelDetails: The task_struct's fdtable is updated.
steps.hardwareDetails: No storage activity; process metadata only.

steps.title: Return the fd to user space
steps.description: The kernel copies the new file descriptor integer back to user space, and execution resumes in the program after open().
steps.kernelDetails: Syscall return path restores registers and mode.
steps.hardwareDetails: CPU transitions back to user mode (ring 3).

steps.title: File is visible in the directory
steps.description: At this point, the new file appears in directory listings (e.g., ls), even if it is still empty.
steps.kernelDetails: Dentry and inode are now part of the VFS tree.
steps.hardwareDetails: Metadata blocks describing the file exist on SSD after commit.

steps.title: write() syscall enters the kernel
steps.description: The program calls write(fd, buf, len), and the CPU executes the syscall instruction to enter the kernel.
steps.kernelDetails: ksys_write() → vfs_write() handle the request.
steps.hardwareDetails: No immediate disk I/O; data still in user memory.

steps.title: Locate inode and address_space
steps.description: The kernel locates the struct file, its inode, and the associated address_space via file->f_mapping->host.
steps.kernelDetails: The mapping determines how offsets map to cache pages.
steps.hardwareDetails: All operations are in memory at this step.

steps.title: Allocate or find page cache folios
steps.description: Using __filemap_get_folio(), the kernel looks for existing cache pages or allocates new folios to hold the file's data.
steps.kernelDetails: folio_alloc() may allocate new pages in RAM.
steps.hardwareDetails: RAM usage grows, but SSD is not touched yet.

steps.title: Copy user data into the page cache
steps.description: The kernel copies bytes from the user buffer into the page cache using _copy_from_user(), populating the new file's in-memory pages.
steps.kernelDetails: User pointers are validated before copying.
steps.hardwareDetails: Only DRAM is accessed; data not yet on SSD.

steps.title: Mark pages dirty
steps.description: set_page_dirty() marks the affected cache pages as dirty so that writeback will eventually flush them to disk.
steps.kernelDetails: Dirty flags inform the writeback code what must be written.
steps.hardwareDetails: No SSD activity yet; state changes are in memory.

steps.title: Allocate on-disk blocks for the file
steps.description: ext4_map_blocks() determines which logical blocks the file should use and updates extent trees or indirect block structures.
steps.kernelDetails: File's on-disk layout is reserved and described.
steps.hardwareDetails: Block bitmaps and extent metadata will be updated on SSD.

steps.title: Update inode size and block counts
steps.description: ext4_mark_iloc_dirty() adjusts fields like i_size and i_blocks to reflect the new data and marks the inode metadata dirty.
steps.kernelDetails: Inode fields now describe the current file contents.
steps.hardwareDetails: Inode blocks will later be flushed to the SSD.

steps.title: Journal metadata for the write
steps.description: jbd2_journal_start() creates a transaction covering inode, extent, and bitmap updates; ext4 in data=ordered mode still writes file data directly, not to the journal.
steps.kernelDetails: Journal buffers collect metadata updates for atomicity.
steps.hardwareDetails: Journal blocks reside in a dedicated area of the SSD.

steps.title: Write dirty data pages to disk (ordered before commit)
steps.description: ext4_writepages() is invoked by writeback to send dirty pages to their final on-disk locations before the journal metadata commit.
steps.kernelDetails: Writeback code clusters writes into larger bios.
steps.hardwareDetails: Data flows through the block layer to the SSD.

steps.title: Commit the ext4 metadata journal for the write
steps.description: jbd2_journal_commit_transaction() writes the commit record for the metadata, ensuring consistency so that data is on disk before metadata points to it.
steps.kernelDetails: Ordered mode guarantees no stale pointers to unwritten data.
steps.hardwareDetails: Sequential journal writes improve SSD performance.

steps.title: Build bios at the block layer
steps.description: submit_bio() and related helpers assemble one or more bios describing which logical blocks to read or write and submit them to the block device queue.
steps.kernelDetails: The generic block layer sees logical block requests only.
steps.hardwareDetails: These requests abstract away SSD-specific details.

steps.title: I/O scheduler queues and optimizes requests
steps.description: Schedulers like mq-deadline or 'none' for NVMe assign tags and order bios, exposing a high-performance queue to the driver.
steps.kernelDetails: blk-mq manages multi-queue I/O submission and completion.
steps.hardwareDetails: Queue depth and ordering influence SSD parallelism.

steps.title: NVMe driver sends commands over PCIe
steps.description: nvme_queue_rq() turns bios into NVMe WRITE commands placed on submission queues, which the SSD controller reads via PCIe.
steps.kernelDetails: Driver manages submission and completion queues and doorbells.
steps.hardwareDetails: PCIe transfers carry data and commands to the SSD.

steps.title: SSD FTL maps logical to physical and programs NAND
steps.description: Inside the SSD, the flash translation layer maps logical block addresses to physical NAND pages, applies ECC, programs cells, and updates mapping tables with wear leveling.
steps.kernelDetails: Opaque to the kernel; treated as a fast block device.
steps.hardwareDetails: Programming a NAND page typically takes 100–500 µs.

steps.title: Mark old pages invalid and schedule GC
steps.description: When overwriting data, the FTL marks previous physical pages invalid and may schedule background garbage collection to reclaim blocks later.
steps.kernelDetails: Kernel is unaware of internal SSD invalidation.
steps.hardwareDetails: Invalid pages accumulate until block erasure.

steps.title: I/O completion interrupt and bio_end_io
steps.description: When the SSD finishes a command, it generates an interrupt; blk_mq_complete_request() and bio_end_io() mark the bio complete.
steps.kernelDetails: Completion handlers wake up waiting tasks or writeback code.
steps.hardwareDetails: NVMe completion queue entries are consumed.

steps.title: Mark pages clean in the page cache
steps.description: clear_page_dirty_for_io() and related helpers clear the dirty flag, turning previously dirty pages into clean ones in the cache.
steps.kernelDetails: The kernel now treats these pages as synced to disk.
steps.hardwareDetails: Data is durably stored on SSD media.

steps.title: fsync() waits for data and metadata to be durable
steps.description: If the program calls fsync(), ext4_sync_file() ensures that all data and relevant metadata have been committed to disk and journal.
steps.kernelDetails: fsync() blocks until lower layers report completion.
steps.hardwareDetails: Ensures power-failure-safe persistence for the file.

steps.title: TRIM/discard frees blocks for reuse on delete
steps.description: When files are deleted or fstrim runs, blkdev_issue_discard() tells the SSD which logical blocks are no longer used so it can erase them in the background.
steps.kernelDetails: Discards help keep SSD performance stable over time.
steps.hardwareDetails: FTL erases entire blocks so pages become ready for reuse.
